transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

They sent me in, mostly. I mean, I came because they told me I had to, but it wasn’t like I was trying to cause a scene or anything.

At the station, I was moving the airway bags around in the bay. I know that sounds stupid when I say it out loud, but they weren’t right where they were, and I could tell they needed to be in a certain pattern. Not just lined up — there was a right order to it. And while I was doing that, the dispatch numbers kept coming through my head, so I was saying them out loud, repeating them, because if I didn’t keep the sequence going it felt like everything in the bay was going to turn bad somehow.

My lieutenant told me to stop, and I heard him, I did, but I couldn’t step away right then. It felt like if I broke it before it was finished, the whole place would… I don’t know, go wrong. Like the balance would be off. So I kept doing it, and then people got upset, and that’s why I’m here.
When this happens, do you believe the danger is truly real, or does part of you know it probably doesn’t make sense?

Part of me knows how it sounds. I know if I say, “the bags have to be in a pattern or something bad happens,” people hear that and think, okay, that doesn’t make sense. But it doesn’t feel made up when it’s happening.

And it’s not just the bags. I know there are people watching me at the station. The injury review people, and some supervisors too. They’ll say it’s routine, like, “Oh, we’re just checking paperwork,” or the cameras are just for security, but I can tell when they’re watching me through the station cameras. And the triage notes — I’ve seen things not look right after, like they’ve been changed around to make me look unsafe, like I don’t know what I’m doing.

So when you ask if the danger is real… I mean, yes, I think it is. Maybe not in the way other people would describe it, but I don’t think I’m just imagining it. I think they’re building something against me, and the paperwork and cameras are part of it.
Do you think it’s possible you could be mistaken about the cameras and paperwork being used against you?

I mean… I guess anything is possible, technically. I know that’s what people want me to say. But sitting here, no, I don’t really think I’m mistaken.

The cameras are there, and I know people say they’re just for security, but I can tell when it’s different. It’s not just that they exist. It’s the timing, the way supervisors bring things up afterward, like they already know what I was doing or where I was standing. And the injury review people, they act like it’s just routine, but it doesn’t feel routine when the same things keep getting questioned and then the paperwork looks… off.

With the triage notes, I know what I wrote. I remember what I put down, and then later it doesn’t look right, like pieces are shifted around or worded in a way that makes me seem unsafe, like I don’t know how to do my job. That’s not just me being sensitive. That’s something being built.

So could I be mistaken? I can say I don’t have every piece of proof in my hand right now, but I don’t think I’m wrong about the cameras and the notes being used against me.
When the need to repeat the numbers or arrange things comes up, does it feel unwanted to you?

Unwanted… I don’t know if that’s exactly the word I’d use. I don’t sit there thinking, “Oh good, I want to do this now.” It’s more like it comes over me, like there’s this pressure that the numbers have to keep going and the bags have to be put in the right pattern, or the bay is going to feel wrong — not just messy, but bad, like something is going to turn.

At the station, when I was moving the airway bags, I knew people were watching and getting irritated, and my lieutenant told me to stop. I heard him. I wasn’t ignoring him like I didn’t care. But stepping away before it was finished felt almost impossible, like breaking the sequence would make the whole place go off-balance. So yes, in that sense I don’t want it, because it gets me in trouble and it looks strange to everyone else. But in the moment it also feels necessary, like I’m supposed to do it and keep repeating the dispatch numbers until it’s right.
When you’re repeating the numbers or arranging the bags, do you do it mainly to relieve a feeling of anxiety or tension?

It’s… partly tension, I guess, but not like I’m just nervous and then I do it and feel better, if that’s what you mean.

At the station, with the airway bags, I kept moving them because there was a pattern that felt right. Not just neat, not just organized — right. And I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, because they had to line up in my head with how the bags were placed. If I stopped in the middle, it felt like the whole bay would go bad somehow, like the sequence would break and then something would be wrong in a way I couldn’t fix.

My lieutenant told me to stop, and I heard him. I knew he was talking to me. But stepping away before it was finished felt impossible. It wasn’t that I was trying to argue with him or make a scene. It was more like if I broke off right then, everything would turn wrong, and I couldn’t make myself leave it unfinished.

So yes, there’s tension, definitely. But it’s more than just relieving anxiety. It feels like I have to complete it because it’s the thing that keeps the bay from going bad.
Do you believe the pattern with the bags really prevents something bad from happening?

I mean… yes, in the moment I do. I know that probably sounds strange when I say it out loud, but when I was there at the station, it didn’t feel like just some habit or me being picky about where the airway bags were.

They sent me here because I kept moving them into this pattern that I knew was right — or I felt it was right, but at the time it was more than a feeling. I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, and the numbers had to match up with how the bags were placed. If one thing was off, the whole bay felt wrong, like it was going to go bad somehow.

My lieutenant told me to stop, and I heard him. I wasn’t ignoring him because I wanted to be difficult. I just couldn’t step away while the sequence was broken. It felt like if I left it unfinished, something bad would happen, or the whole place would sort of turn wrong. I don’t know how to explain it better than that. It wasn’t a normal thought like, “If I move this bag, then this exact thing won’t happen.” It was more like I knew I had to finish it or things wouldn’t be safe.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I’ve had, like, a clear person standing there talking to me when nobody’s there, if that’s what you mean.

Sometimes when things are quiet, especially after a lot of stress, I’ll think I heard something and then I’ll look around and there isn’t anyone, but I don’t know if that counts as a voice or just my mind catching on sounds. I don’t want to say yes to something if I’m not sure, because “hearing voices” sounds very specific, like words coming from outside my head. I haven’t noticed it like that, not in a way I can clearly point to.
Do you believe other people would be safer if you did not arrange the bags and repeat the numbers?

I think… yes, that’s what it felt like at the station. Not in a clean, logical way where I could explain, “This bag here means that person is safer,” but if I didn’t arrange them, and if I didn’t keep saying the dispatch numbers until they lined up right in my head, then the bay felt unsafe. Like something in it would go bad.

That’s why they sent me here, really. I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern, and I knew it was the right pattern, or at least it felt so strongly right that I couldn’t treat it like a preference. And I was repeating the numbers out loud, not quietly enough, I guess, because people noticed. My lieutenant told me to stop, and I understood him, but I couldn’t just leave it halfway done. It felt like breaking the sequence would make everything wrong, and then other people wouldn’t be safe.

So… yes. In that moment, I believed arranging them and repeating the numbers was connected to keeping things safe. Even saying that now, I know how it sounds, but that was the reason I couldn’t step away.
When you feel you have to arrange the bags or repeat the numbers, do those thoughts feel like your own thoughts?

They feel like mine, I think… but not mine in the normal way. That’s the part that’s hard to explain.

It’s not like somebody else is putting a sentence in my head, at least I don’t think that’s what’s happening. It starts in me, like I notice the bags aren’t in the right place, or I hear the dispatch numbers in my mind and then I start saying them out loud because they have to line up. But once it starts, it doesn’t feel like an ordinary thought I can just choose to ignore. It gets bigger than that.

At the station, when they sent me here, I kept moving the airway bags into that pattern because I knew it was right. Or… I knew it at the time. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant told me to stop, and I heard him, I understood what he wanted. But I couldn’t step away from it. It felt like if I broke the sequence or left it unfinished, the whole bay would go bad somehow.

So yes, they feel like my thoughts, but they don’t feel voluntary. They feel like they come with this pressure behind them, like I have to follow them until the pattern is right.
When you are not in the middle of arranging the bags, do you believe that putting them in that pattern truly prevents harm?

When I’m not right in the middle of it… I can sort of see that it doesn’t make normal sense. Like if you asked me sitting here, calmly, “Does putting the airway bags in that exact pattern literally prevent harm?” I don’t know that I could defend it like a real rule or a protocol.

But at the station, it didn’t feel optional. They sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern, the one that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud over and over. My lieutenant told me to stop, and I heard him, I knew he meant stop, but I couldn’t step away because it felt like if I broke the sequence before it was finished, the whole bay would go bad somehow.

So when I’m away from it, I can question it more. But when it starts, it feels true enough that I act like it’s true. That’s probably the best way I can say it.
Right now, do you believe for certain that supervisors are using the cameras and paperwork against you?

Right now? Yes. I mean… I know that sounds like I’m supposed to say, “I’m not certain,” because everyone keeps calling it routine review or paperwork, but that’s not how it feels from where I’m standing.

I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. Not just casually, not like normal security footage that sits there unless something happens. Watching me. Checking what I do, how I move things, how long I stand in one place, whether I look unsafe. And then the paperwork part… the triage notes, the things I wrote, they don’t always feel like they stay the way I put them. It feels like they’re changing them, or presenting them in a way that makes me look unsafe or unreliable.

They tell me it’s just routine, that injury reviews have forms and supervisors check documentation, and I understand those words. I know that’s what they say. But it doesn’t match what I can see happening. The cameras, the notes, the way people get quiet after reviewing things—it all lines up too much.

So yes, right now I do believe they’re using the cameras and the paperwork against me. I’m not saying that because I want trouble with them. I don’t. I just don’t think it’s innocent.
Do you believe anyone is able to put thoughts into your mind?

I don’t know. I mean, I don’t think I can say yes to that the way you’re asking it.

Like… I don’t have a clear sense of someone taking a thought and putting it into my head like a radio signal or something. That’s not really how it feels to me. The thoughts feel like they happen inside me, even when they get too strong or they don’t feel normal. I can get stuck on them, and they can feel like they have this pressure behind them, but I’m not sure that means someone else put them there.

Sometimes I wonder where they come from, because they don’t feel like regular thinking. They don’t feel calm, or chosen, or like I can just say, “No, I’m not doing that.” But if you’re asking if I believe a person can directly insert thoughts into my mind… I haven’t noticed it like that. I’m not saying nothing strange is happening, just that I can’t point to it and say, “That thought came from that person and they placed it there.”
When the urge to arrange the bags or repeat the numbers comes up, do you try to resist it?

I try to, yes. I mean, I tell myself, “Don’t do it, just leave the bags where they are, stop saying the numbers,” but once it gets going it’s like resisting makes it louder.

At the station, that’s why they sent me here. I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern that I knew was right, or that felt right—like the spacing and the order had to be exact—and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Not just once. Over and over, because if I lost the sequence, I felt like I had to start it again.

My lieutenant told me to stop. I heard him. I wasn’t confused about what he wanted. I knew he was standing there telling me to step away, and part of me knew I should just back off because it was becoming a problem. But I couldn’t. It felt like if I stopped before it was finished, if I broke the pattern or left the bags wrong, then the whole bay would go bad somehow. Like something unsafe would happen and it would be because I didn’t complete it.

So I do try to resist, but in the moment it doesn’t feel like a normal choice. It feels like I’m holding back something bad by doing it, and stopping feels worse than getting in trouble.
Do you believe for certain that the bad thing would really happen if you did not finish arranging the bags?

Certain is hard, because if I say “certain,” it sounds like I’m claiming I can prove it, and I can’t prove it the way you’d prove something on paper. But in the moment, when I’m standing there with the airway bags and the numbers are in my head, it feels certain enough that I can’t walk away.

That’s why they sent me here. I kept moving the bags into the pattern that felt right—like the exact order and spacing mattered—and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud because the sequence had to stay intact. My lieutenant was telling me to stop and step away, and I heard him, I understood him, but it felt like if I broke it before it was finished, the whole bay would go bad somehow.

I don’t mean I had a clear picture like, “This exact accident will happen at this exact time.” It’s more like this heavy, awful knowing that something unsafe would happen if I left it wrong. Like the bay would be off, contaminated almost, not physically maybe, but wrong in a way that could turn into something bad. And if I didn’t finish arranging the bags, then it would be on me.

So… do I believe for certain? When I’m calm, sitting here, I can say maybe I don’t know for certain. But when it’s happening, yes, it feels real enough that stopping feels impossible.
When the urge starts, do you feel the thought is unreasonable?

Yeah… I mean, part of me does. That’s the confusing thing. There’s a part of me that can hear how it sounds when I say it out loud—like, “If I don’t put the airway bags in the right pattern, the whole bay is going to go bad.” I know that sounds unreasonable sitting here, especially when I’m trying to explain it to you calmly.

But when the urge starts, it doesn’t feel unreasonable in the moment. It feels urgent. It feels like I’ve noticed something everyone else is missing, like the order is wrong and if I don’t fix it, something unsafe is going to happen. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags because the spacing and the pattern had to be right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud because if I lost the sequence, it felt like everything would come apart.

My lieutenant told me to stop, and I understood him. I wasn’t ignoring him because I didn’t care. I just couldn’t step away, because stopping before it felt finished felt worse than continuing. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go wrong somehow.

So… yes, I can see it might be unreasonable afterward, or from the outside. But when it starts, it feels real enough that I don’t trust myself to leave it alone.
If someone showed you clear proof that the cameras and notes were not being used against you, would you believe it?

I don’t think I would, not right away. I know that probably sounds like I’m being stubborn, but if someone just came in and said, “Here, this proves the cameras aren’t being used like that,” I’d be thinking, who put that together? Who had access to it? What part are they not showing me?

Because it’s not just the cameras by themselves. It’s the way the injury review people look at things after the fact, and then some of the supervisors act like it’s all routine, like it’s just paperwork or a quality check. But then my triage notes don’t read the way I remember writing them, or things are emphasized in a way that makes me look unsafe, like I missed something or shouldn’t have been trusted. And when they tell me, “No, that’s just the normal review process,” it doesn’t feel normal to me. It feels like they already decided what they want me to look like, and they’re using the cameras and the notes to build that.

So if you showed me proof, I’d have to know where it came from. I’d need more than one person saying it. And even then, I’d probably still wonder if the proof was part of the same thing. Like, if the same people who can watch through the station cameras and change the documentation are also the people telling me nothing happened, then I don’t know how I’m supposed to trust that.

I’m not trying to argue with you. I just… I know what it looks like from my side. They say it’s routine paperwork, but it feels like they’re using it against me.
Aside from the cameras and paperwork, do you believe anyone is trying to harm you or plot against you?

I don’t know if I’d say “harm” like someone is going to jump me in the parking lot or something. That’s not really what I mean. It’s more… they’re trying to make me look unsafe. Like they’re building something around me, piece by piece, so later they can point to it and say, “See, he shouldn’t have been trusted.”

The injury review people, and some of the supervisors, they’ve been watching through the station cameras. I know they say the cameras are just there for normal reasons, security or whatever, and that the reviews are routine paperwork, but that’s not how it feels from my side. It feels directed. Like they’re looking for certain things, clipping things together in their heads, and then the triage notes don’t match the way I remember them. They read different, or they emphasize things in a way that makes me look like I missed something.

So, plotting against me… yeah, in that sense. Not like some movie thing, not everyone in the station, not some huge conspiracy. But I do think certain people are using the cameras and the paperwork against me. They can call it routine all they want, but when the notes make me look unsafe and the camera review lines up with that, it feels like they’re trying to set the record a certain way. And once it’s written like that, once it’s in the file, it’s hard to undo.
Have you ever believed that supervisors could actually alter your triage notes after you submitted them?

Yes. I mean… yes, I have believed that. Not just “could,” like some abstract possibility. I’ve felt pretty sure that it has happened.

That’s part of what scares me, because once I submit those triage notes, they’re supposed to reflect what I saw and what I did, right? They’re supposed to be my documentation. But then later, when something is being reviewed, the notes don’t feel like mine anymore. They read wrong. Not always in some obvious way where a whole paragraph is different, but the emphasis is off, or something is framed like I was careless, like I missed something important, like I shouldn’t have been trusted on the call.

And when I’ve tried to bring it up, people act like it’s just routine paperwork, or quality review, or injury review doing what they always do. But I know the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras, and then the notes line up with that same story they’re trying to make — that I’m unsafe. It feels coordinated. Like they watch something on camera, decide what it means, and then the documentation somehow starts supporting that version.

I know how that sounds. I know you might say there are audit trails or policies or whatever. But from my side, it doesn’t feel like a mistake. It feels like they’re changing things after I submit them so the record makes me look worse. And once it’s in the record, people believe the record over me.
How long have you believed that supervisors were using the cameras and your notes against you?

It’s been about two months, I think. Around there. It wasn’t like one day I woke up and had the whole thing figured out in my head, but the camera stuff and the notes not feeling right, and the way people at the station started acting around it — that’s been going on for maybe the last two months.

At first I tried to tell myself it was just normal review stuff, like maybe I was overreading it because the job is stressful and there’s always paperwork after calls. But then it kept lining up — the cameras, the injury review people, the way supervisors would talk like everything was routine, and then the documentation would seem to point in the same direction. That’s when it started feeling like it wasn’t just random.

So, yeah… roughly two months. Long enough that it doesn’t feel like a one-time misunderstanding anymore.
Do you believe anyone can read your thoughts?

I don’t think so. Not in the sense that someone can literally hear what I’m thinking word for word, like I’m broadcasting it. I haven’t noticed that exactly.

I mean, sometimes people seem to know what I’m worried about before I say it, but that could be because of how I’m acting, or because they already know the situation. I don’t want to say something I’m not sure about. The camera stuff and the paperwork, that feels more concrete to me than someone reading my thoughts.

So… no, I don’t really believe people can read my thoughts. At least not that I can say for sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences intrusive thoughts as unwanted and tries to resist them, which best distinguishes OCD with poor insight from a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: When the need to repeat the numbers or arrange things comes up, does it feel unwanted to you?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: They sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern I knew was right, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence.

patient.answer:
Unwanted… I don’t know if that’s exactly the word I’d use.
